extracted.intended_audience: general readers and writers of classic comic/digressive fiction; students of literature
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and implicit principles for composing and characterizing in long-form comic, digressive narrative (à la Sterne). Emphasizes characterization by contrast, use of metaphor and ornament, spontaneity over rigid planning, and maintenance of distinct recurring motifs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soldier's geography knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: A soldier 'must be acquainted intimately with every country and its boundaries where his profession carries him; he should know every town and city, and village and hamlet, with the canals, the roads, and hollow ways which lead up to them; there is not a river or a rivulet he passes, _Trim_, but he should be able at first sight to tell thee what is its name—in what mountains it takes its rise—what is its course—how far it is navigable—where fordable—where not; he should know the fertility of every valley, as well as the hind who ploughs it; and be able to describe, or, if it is required, to give thee an exact map of all the plains and defiles, the forts, the acclivities, the woods and morasses, thro' and by which his army is to march; he should know their produce, their plants, their minerals, their waters, their animals, their seasons, their climates, their heats and cold, their inhabitants, their customs, their language, their policy, and even their religion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists concrete items a soldier ought to know (places, roads, watercourses and fords, topography of marches, agricultural fertility, flora and fauna, natural resources, seasons/climate, inhabitants' customs/languages/politics/religion). Framed as essential for planning marches and operations (example: Marlborough's campaigns could not advance without Geography).

rubrics_metrics.name: Chronology's limited but crucial importance (military context)
rubrics_metrics.description: Chronology 'seems a science which the soldier might best spare, was it not for the lights which that science must one day give him, in determining the invention of powder...the world cannot be too exact in ascertaining the precise time of its discovery, or too inquisitive in knowing what great man was the discoverer.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chronology may be less immediately practical for soldiers than geography, but it matters for dating major technological shifts (e.g., gunpowder) that alter tactics and defences. Use historical dating to understand eras of military change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid acting or writing strictly by plan
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrator: 'consider, sir, what nonsense it is, either in fighting, or writing, or any thing else (whether in rhyme to it, or not) which a man has occasion to do—To act by plan.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A rigid plan, independent of circumstances, can obstruct effectiveness; adapt tactics and composition to changing circumstances. The example: Mrs. Wadman's fixed 'PLAN' for attacking the sentry-box is ill-suited and 'opposed every impression she could make' — showing that slavish adherence to a preconceived plan can undermine the intended effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reveal character by contrasting manners under the same event
rubrics_metrics.description: 'There is nothing shews the character of my father and my uncle Toby, in a more entertaining light, than their different manner of deportment, under the same accident.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To characterize effectively, present two (or more) characters facing the same situation and let their differing reactions expose temperament and moral makeup. Contrast is an entertaining and revealing technique for characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep recurring motifs and characters distinct
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrator: 'I must here observe to you the difference betwixt My father's ass and my hobby-horse—in order to keep characters as separate as may be, in our fancies as we go along.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain clarity between an author's recurring personal obsessions (hobby-horse: playful, ephemeral amusements) and genuine character flaws/vices (the father's 'ass') so that recurring elements serve distinct narrative purposes and do not conflate or confuse the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use apt metaphor and place it for both ornament and use
rubrics_metrics.description: 'AN eye is for all the world exactly like a cannon, in this respect; That it is not so much the eye or the cannon, in themselves, as it is the carriage of the eye—and the carriage of the cannon...I don’t think the comparison a bad one: However, as ’tis made and placed at the head of the chapter, as much for use as ornament...'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ bold, apt comparisons (metaphors) that illuminate a trait (e.g., eyes and cannons) and consider their placement (chapter headings, openings) to serve both decorative and functional narrative purposes. The 'carriage' (manner of presentation) often matters more than the object compared.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise restraint in descriptive praise
rubrics_metrics.description: Narratorial aside: 'But I shall be in love with it myself, if I say another word about it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice restraint: avoid over-elaboration or excessive encomium that might distract or reduce the effect. Withhold some description to keep the reader's imagination engaged and to avoid self-indulgent prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match tactics/devices to the emotional or rhetorical effect desired
rubrics_metrics.description: On Mrs. Wadman's attempted attack: the 'manœuvre of fingers and hands in the attack of the sentry-box, was so outdone by that of the fair Beguine's...that just then, that particular attack, however successful before—became the most heartless attack that could be made.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When staging a scene (romantic, comic, or dramatic), choose gestures/devices that fit and enhance the emotional tenor; a previously successful tactic can fail if it is mismatched to the present context or outshone by another example. Tailor technique to scene-specific dynamics.
